title: Gulveer Singh Ran a 3:55 Mile. He Is the First Indian to Break the Four-Minute Barrier. He Did It in Cleveland.
excerpt: The army runner's historic performance capped a week in which Indian athletes shattered barriers across the 100m, 400m, mile, high jump, and decathlon — all within days of each other.
body:
Gulveer Singh has spent the last two years quietly rewriting Indian distance running records from a training base in the United States. On Saturday, at the 24th Annual Music City Track Carnival in Cleveland, he did something no Indian had ever done: he ran a mile in under four minutes.

His time of 3:55.63 was not a fringe achievement. Gulveer won the Men's 1 Mile Pro event outright, finishing ahead of Americans Christopher Knight (3:59.72) and Tristan Trevino (4:00.27). The 27-year-old from the Indian Army did not merely break the barrier — he cleared it with daylight to spare.

## The Significance of Four Minutes

The four-minute mile is one of sport's most iconic benchmarks. When Roger Bannister first broke it in 1954, it was considered a limit of human performance. Since then, more than 1,800 runners worldwide have gone under. But until last Saturday, not a single Indian was among them.

India is a country of 1.4 billion people. It has produced world-class athletes in cricket, badminton, shooting, wrestling, and javelin. But middle-distance running has historically been a blindspot — an event where neither the national federation's attention nor the country's training infrastructure has produced globally competitive athletes.

Gulveer's breakthrough was not accidental. He trains full-time in the United States, where access to high-quality tracks, coaching, competition, and altitude training is routine. His résumé already included being the first Indian to break 13 minutes for the indoor 5,000m (12:59.77 at the Boston University Terrier DMR Challenge in 2025) and the national 10,000m record of 27:00.22. The sub-four mile was the logical next frontier.

## A Week of Broken Barriers

What makes Gulveer's achievement even more striking is the context. His performance came during an extraordinary week for Indian athletics, one in which multiple historical barriers fell almost simultaneously.

At the Federation Cup in Ranchi, Gurindervir Singh clocked 10.09 seconds in the 100m — the first Indian to go under 10.10. The sprint has long been Indian athletics' most frustrating event, with generations of athletes falling just short of globally competitive times. Gurindervir's run secured qualification for both the Glasgow Commonwealth Games and the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.

In the 400m, Vishal TK ran 44.98 seconds — the first Indian to break the 45-second barrier. And in the decathlon, Tejaswin Shankar crossed 8,000 points for the first time by an Indian athlete, a threshold that separates continental-level performers from world-class all-rounders.

Meanwhile, at the Asian U20 Athletics Championships in Hong Kong, high jumper Pooja cleared 1.93m to win gold and break a decade-old national record of 1.92m set by Sahana Kumari in 2012. Her jump also surpassed the previous Asian U20 meet record.

Five events. Five barriers. One week.

## The NRI Training Model

Gulveer's story is, in many ways, a diaspora story. He is an Indian Army athlete who trains in the United States. The pattern is not new — Neeraj Chopra trained extensively in Europe before winning Olympic gold in the javelin, and several Indian distance runners have moved to American collegiate and professional training groups in recent years.

The model works because the US offers what India currently cannot: year-round access to World Athletics Continental Tour events, consistent competition against high-calibre fields, and the logistical support that allows athletes to race frequently without the disruption of international travel from South Asia.

For NRIs who follow Indian athletics, Gulveer's run in Cleveland carries an extra resonance. It happened not at a major championships or a stadium in India, but at a mid-tier meet on an American university campus — the kind of low-key, high-performance environment where records are quietly broken while the sports world looks elsewhere.

## What Comes Next

Gulveer is preparing for the Glasgow Commonwealth Games (July 23 to August 2) and the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan (September 19 to October 4). Based on his current form, he is a genuine medal contender in the 5,000m and 10,000m at both events.

The broader question for Indian athletics is whether this week of record-breaking represents a systemic shift or a cluster of individual breakthroughs. The answer may not matter to the athletes themselves. They are running, jumping, and throwing at levels that were considered impossible for Indians a generation ago.

Gulveer Singh's time of 3:55.63 will stand in the record books. But the real milestone is simpler: an Indian ran a mile in under four minutes. It took 72 years longer than it should have. It will not be the last.
author: Diaspora Desk
